• Design, develop and lead to the production of state-of-the-art sensors, weapon systems, platforms and allied equipment for our Defence Services.

• Develop infrastructure and committed quality manpower and build strong indigenous technology base.

• The act aimed to strengthen the concept of India as a secular state by explicitly including the word **"Secular"** in the Preamble.
 
• It was enacted during the tenure of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in the context of the Emergency period.
 
• The changes brought by the amendment emphasized the importance of secularism in ensuring equality and non-discrimination based on religion.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Secularism in India:**

 
 
• Secularism in India means that the state treats all religions equally and ensures freedom of religion.
 
• It prohibits discrimination based on religion and ensures protection of minority rights.
 
• The concept is enshrined under Articles 25 to 28 of the Indian Constitution.
 
 
 
• **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act Highlights:**
 
 
• It introduced changes to the Seventh Schedule, enhancing the power of the central government.
 
• It brought provisions related to the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), emphasizing the role of the state in promoting welfare.
 
• It curtailed judicial review by limiting the scope of fundamental rights during the Emergency.
 
 
 
• **Voting Age Lowering:**
 
 
• The voting age in India was reduced from 21 to 18 through the **61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988**, not the 42nd Amendment.
 
 
 
• **Anti-Defection Law:**
 
 
• The Anti-Defection Law was introduced by the **52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985**, not the 42nd Amendment.
 
• It aimed to curb political defections and ensure stability in governments.

questions.question: In which year was the 42nd Amendment in the Indian Constitution passed?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**1976**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The **42nd Amendment** of the Indian Constitution was enacted in the year **1976**.
 
• This amendment is known as the "**Mini Constitution**" because it brought about a major transformation in the Constitution.
 
• It was introduced during the tenure of **Prime Minister Indira Gandhi**.
 
• The amendment was passed during the **Emergency period**, which lasted from **1975 to 1977**.
 
• It made significant changes to the Constitution, including the inclusion of the words "**Socialist**" and "**Secular**" in the Preamble, emphasizing the nation's character.
 
• It also added a new chapter on "**Fundamental Duties**" for citizens under Part IVA of the Constitution (Article 51A).
 
• The amendment increased the powers of the **central government** and curtailed the rights of the judiciary.
 
• It altered the **Directive Principles of State Policy** and strengthened laws to prevent anti-national activities.
 
• The amendment introduced provisions for the **duration of Lok Sabha and State Assemblies**, extending their tenure from 5 years to 6 years, though this was later reversed by the **44th Amendment**.

questions.question: What does Article 164 of the Indian Constitution state about the appointment of the Chief Minister?

options.text: The Chief Minister shall be appointed by the Governor.
The Chief Minister is elected by the legislative assembly of the state.
The Chief Minister is chosen through a referendum in the state.
The Chief Minister is appointed by the President of India.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The Chief Minister shall be appointed by the Governor.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 164 of the Indian Constitution specifies that the Chief Minister shall be appointed by the Governor of the state.
 
• The Governor appoints the Chief Minister based on the leader of the majority party in the state legislative assembly.
 
• If no single party has a majority, the Governor may appoint a Chief Minister who he believes can secure a majority in the assembly.
 
• The Chief Minister, once appointed, advises the Governor on the appointment of other ministers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Governor's Role:**

 
 
• The Governor is the constitutional head of a state in India, appointed by the President of India.
 
• One of the Governor's key responsibilities is to ensure that a stable government is formed in the state.
 
 
 
• **State Legislative Assembly:**
 
 
• The state legislative assembly is the lower house of the state legislature in India.
 
• Members of the legislative assembly (MLAs) are directly elected by the people of the state.
 
 
 
• **Majority Party:**
 
 
• The party with the majority of seats in the legislative assembly is typically invited to form the government.
 
• The leader of the majority party is usually appointed as the Chief Minister.
 
 
 
• **Cabinet of Ministers:**
 
 
• The Chief Minister heads the state cabinet, which consists of ministers appointed on the Chief Minister's advice.
 
• The cabinet is responsible for the day-to-day administration of the state.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India says that all public places are open to all citizens?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 15(2)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 15(2)** of the Indian Constitution specifically prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth in access to public places.
 
• This provision ensures that all citizens have equal rights to access public spaces such as parks, restaurants, hotels, and places of entertainment.
 
• Article 15(2) aims at removing social barriers and promoting inclusivity, thereby upholding the ideals of equality enshrined in the Constitution.
 
• It is part of the broader **Right to Equality** guaranteed under Articles 14 to 18 of the Constitution.
 
• Article 15(2) complements Article 17, which abolishes untouchability and ensures no discrimination in public places based on caste.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 14:** Guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.
 
• **Article 15(1):** Prohibits discrimination by the State against any citizen on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.
 
• **Article 16:** Provides for equality of opportunity in matters of public employment and prohibits discrimination based on religion, race, caste, sex, descent, or place of birth.
 
• **Article 17:** Abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form, ensuring access to public places without caste-based discrimination.
 
• **Fundamental Rights:** Articles 12 to 35 of the Constitution collectively define the fundamental rights guaranteed to every citizen, ensuring dignity and equality.

questions.question: 'Equal pay for equal work is prevention of concentration of wealth' is mentioned under which Article of the Indian Constitution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 39**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 39 of the Indian Constitution falls under the **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**.
 
• It directs the State to ensure that wealth and resources are not concentrated in a manner detrimental to the common good.
 
• The provision aims to secure **equal pay for equal work** for both men and women.
 
• It promotes policies that provide adequate means of livelihood for all citizens and prevent exploitation.
 
• Article 39 emphasizes social justice and economic equality as foundational principles for governance in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP):**

 
 
• DPSPs are non-justiciable guidelines provided in Part IV of the Constitution (Articles 36-51).
 
• The purpose of DPSPs is to establish a framework for achieving socio-economic justice and equitable governance.
 
 
 
• **Equal Pay for Equal Work:**
 
 
• It is a principle aimed at eliminating discrimination in wage payments based on gender or other factors.
 
• This concept is also recognized as a fundamental labor right under international conventions like the ILO.
 
 
 
• **Concentration of Wealth:**
 
 
• Concentration of wealth refers to the unequal distribution of economic resources among individuals or groups.
 
• Article 39 aims to prevent this by promoting equitable distribution through policies and laws.
 
 
 
• **Social and Economic Justice:**
 
 
• Social justice ensures fair treatment for all citizens, while economic justice aims to reduce inequalities in wealth and income.
 
• These concepts are central to the DPSPs and are integral to achieving the goals of the Indian Constitution.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution provides for the establishment of a Legislative Assembly in a Union Territory?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Article 239A**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 239A** of the Indian Constitution provides for the establishment of a **Legislative Assembly** in certain **Union Territories**, such as Puducherry.
 
• This Article was inserted by the **Constitution (Fourteenth Amendment) Act, 1962**.
 
• The legislative assembly established under this Article has the power to make laws on subjects mentioned in the **State List** and the **Concurrent List** for that Union Territory.
 
• It also allows for the creation of a **Council of Ministers** to aid and advise the administrator of the Union Territory.
 
• Initially, this provision was applicable to both **Puducherry** and **Himachal Pradesh**, but with Himachal Pradesh attaining statehood in 1971, it now applies only to Puducherry.
 
• This Article is an example of the flexibility of the Indian Constitution to accommodate the **unique administrative requirements** of Union Territories.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 241**__

 __
 
• **Article 241** deals with the establishment of **High Courts** for Union Territories.
 
• This Article provides that Parliament may establish or abolish High Courts for Union Territories through legislation.
 
• It is significant in ensuring **judicial administration** in regions without their own state High Courts.
 
 
 
• **Article 239**__
 __
 
• **Article 239** outlines the administration of Union Territories by the **President of India** through an administrator appointed by him.
 
• It provides the general framework for governance in Union Territories which do not have a Legislative Assembly.
 
• This Article ensures that Union Territories are under the direct **control and supervision** of the Central Government.
 
 
 
• **Article 240**__
 
 
• **Article 240** empowers the President to make regulations for certain Union Territories, such as **Lakshadweep, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, and Daman and Diu.**
 
• These regulations have the same effect as laws made by the Legislative Assembly of a state.
 
• This Article is used in Union Territories that do not have a Legislative Assembly and require governance through Presidential regulations.

questions.question: Admission and allocation of new states is mentioned in which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Article 2**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 2** of the Indian Constitution deals with the **admission and establishment** of new states into the Union of India.
 
• It empowers **Parliament** to make laws for the admission or establishment of new states.
 
• The **Parliament** has the authority to determine the terms and conditions for such admission or establishment.
 
• This article is significant for the **expansion of the Indian Union**, ensuring that the Constitution allows flexibility for adding new states.
 
• Examples include the integration of territories like **Sikkim** into India, which was facilitated under provisions of Article 2.
 
• It provides a constitutional framework for the **reorganization and territorial expansion** of India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 3**__

 __
 
• **Article 3** of the Indian Constitution deals with the **formation of new states** and **alteration of areas, boundaries, and names** of existing states.
 
• It allows **Parliament** to reorganize the states within India by **merging, splitting, or modifying boundaries**, but requires the **President** to first refer the matter to the concerned state legislature for its opinion.
 
• This article is distinct from **Article 2**, as it focuses on the internal reorganization of states rather than the admission of new ones.
 
 
 
• **Article 4**__
 __
 
• **Article 4** provides that laws made under **Articles 2 and 3** relating to admission or reorganization of states are not considered amendments to the Constitution under **Article 368**.
 
• It ensures that such laws can be enacted through **ordinary legislative procedures**, without requiring a **special amendment process**.
 
 
 
• **Article 1**__
 
 
• **Article 1** defines **India** as a "Union of States" and outlines the **territory of India**.
 
• It specifies that India comprises **states, union territories**, and any other territories that may be acquired.

• The council can be constituted by the **President of India** if it appears necessary for better coordination between the states.
 
• The key functions of the council include **investigation and discussion** of subjects of common interest between states, recommendations for better policy implementation, and addressing disputes.
 
• The inter-state council helps in ensuring **smooth functioning** of India's federal structure by creating a platform for dialogue and resolution.
 
• This provision reflects the importance of maintaining harmony and cooperation among states to achieve **national objectives**.

 __
 
• **Article 270** pertains to the distribution of **tax revenues** between the central government and the states.
 
• This article allows for certain taxes to be collected by the union and then shared with the states.
 
• The division of revenues is determined based on recommendations by the **Finance Commission.**
 
 
 
• **Article 275**__
 __
 
• **Article 275** provides for **grants-in-aid** to the states from the Consolidated Fund of India.
 
• These grants are given to states for specific purposes such as improving administration or addressing special needs.
 
• It emphasizes the financial assistance from the union to states for equitable development.
 
 
 
• **Article 256**__

• This article highlights the importance of maintaining **constitutional harmony** between the union and state governments.

questions.question: Article 356 deals with which of the following provisions of the Indian Constitution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**President's Rule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 356 of the Indian Constitution empowers the President of India to impose **President's Rule** in a state if the constitutional machinery breaks down.
 
• President's Rule can be imposed based on the report of the **Governor** or otherwise if the President is satisfied that governance in a state cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution.
 
• During President's Rule, the state legislature is suspended, and the powers of the state government are exercised by the President through the Governor or an appointed administrator.
 
• The imposition of President's Rule is subject to **Parliamentary approval** and can initially remain in force for six months, extendable up to three years under specific conditions.
 
• President's Rule is often seen as a measure to maintain constitutional order but has been criticized for misuse in the past.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Constitutional Provisions Related to Emergency:**

 
 
• Article 352: National Emergency due to war, external aggression, or armed rebellion.
 
• Article 356: State Emergency or President's Rule due to the failure of constitutional machinery in a state.
 
• Article 360: Financial Emergency due to a threat to India's financial stability or credit.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• The first instance of President's Rule occurred in **Punjab in 1951**.
 
• President's Rule has been imposed in states more than **100 times** since the Constitution came into effect.
 
• Critics argue it has been used as a tool for political purposes rather than genuine constitutional crises.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Safeguards:**
 
 
• The Supreme Court, in the **S.R. Bommai case (1994)**, laid down strict guidelines for imposing President's Rule.
 
• The Court held that the proclamation of President's Rule is subject to judicial review.
 
• It emphasized that the imposition must be based on objective material and not arbitrary decisions.
 
 
 
• **Key Implications:**
 
 
• State governments lose their autonomy temporarily, and governance is taken over by the central government.
 
• It is seen as a last-resort mechanism to uphold constitutional governance in states.
 
• Parliamentary approval acts as a check to ensure accountability in its imposition.

questions.question: Under which Article of the Indian Constitution does the Supreme Court have the power to grant Special Leave to Appeal?

options.text: Article 143 of the Constitution of India
Article 136 of the Constitution of India
Article 226 of the Constitution of India
Article 124 of the Constitution of India

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 136 of the Constitution of India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 136** of the Indian Constitution provides the Supreme Court with the discretionary power to grant **Special Leave to Appeal** against any judgment, decree, or order passed by any court or tribunal in India (except military tribunals).
 
• This power is considered an **extraordinary jurisdiction** and is invoked in cases involving substantial questions of law or grave injustice.
 
• The provision does not serve as a regular appellate jurisdiction but as a **residual power** to ensure justice and correct errors of law or fact.
 
• Special Leave Petition (SLP) under Article 136 is not a matter of right but a privilege granted by the Supreme Court at its discretion.
 
• This Article emphasizes the Supreme Court's role as the **guardian of the Constitution** and the protector of fundamental rights.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Judicial Review in India:**

 
 
• The Supreme Court has the power of judicial review to ensure that laws and executive actions do not violate the Constitution.
 
• Articles 32, 136, 226, and 227 are key provisions ensuring judicial review of legislative and executive actions.
 
 
 
• **Structure of the Indian Judiciary:**
 
 
• The Indian judiciary is a unified and independent system with the Supreme Court at the apex, followed by High Courts and subordinate courts.
 
• The Supreme Court has original, appellate, and advisory jurisdictions.
 
 
 
• **Role of the Supreme Court as a Court of Record:**
 
 
• Under Article 129, the Supreme Court is a Court of Record, meaning its judgments are authoritative and act as precedents.
 
• The Court also has the power to punish for its contempt.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Article 226:**
 
 
• While Article 136 deals with the Supreme Court's discretionary power, Article 226 provides High Courts the power to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights and other legal rights.
 
• Article 226 is broader in scope compared to Article 32 as it extends to legal rights, not just fundamental rights.

questions.question: Who among the following has the power to enforce the Fundamental Rights under Article 32?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Supreme Court**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Under **Article 32** of the Indian Constitution, the **Supreme Court** has the power to enforce Fundamental Rights.
 
• It is often referred to as the "heart and soul" of the Constitution by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
 
• Article 32 provides the right to individuals to move the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of their Fundamental Rights.
 
• The Supreme Court can issue **five types of writs** for the enforcement of these rights: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto.
 
• This Article makes the Supreme Court the ultimate protector and guarantor of Fundamental Rights in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights:**

 
 
• They are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution and are essential for the development of individuals.
 
• There are six categories of Fundamental Rights: Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies.
 
 
 
• **Writs:**
 
 
• **Habeas Corpus**: To release a person detained unlawfully.
 
• **Mandamus**: To direct a public authority to perform its duty.
 
• **Prohibition**: To stop a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction.
 
• **Certiorari**: To transfer a case from a lower court to a higher court for review.
 
• **Quo Warranto**: To challenge the legality of a person holding a public office.
 
 
 
• **Role of Judiciary:**
 
 
• The judiciary acts as the guardian of the Constitution and ensures that no law or action violates Fundamental Rights.
 
• High Courts also have the power to issue writs under Article 226 of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Article 32:**

questions.question: Which of the following Articles allows the State to make special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes?

• **Article 15 (4):**

• Empowers the State to make special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes, SC, and ST.
 
 
 
• **Article 16:**
 
 
• Provides for equality of opportunity in public employment.
 
• Allows reservations for backward classes in services under the State.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of Part IV of the Indian Constitution has a provision for the separation of Judiciary from the Executive?

__

• The objective of this provision is to ensure the independence of the judiciary, which is essential for a fair and impartial justice system.
 
• This separation is considered a cornerstone of the doctrine of the rule of law and is vital for maintaining checks and balances in governance.
 
• Article 50 is not enforceable by the courts but serves as a guiding principle for the State to implement through legislation.

• **Judiciary-Executive Separation:** The separation ensures that judicial decisions are free from political or administrative influences, promoting impartiality.
 
• **Rule of Law:** A fundamental principle in governance where every individual, including the government, is subject to the law.
 
• **Judicial Independence:** Essential for democracy, it ensures that judges are free to make decisions based solely on law and facts, without external pressure.
 
• **Implementation:** While Article 50 is not legally enforceable, various laws and reforms (e.g., the Criminal Procedure Code amendments) have been introduced to achieve this separation over time.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of ministers, including the Chief Minister, allowed in a state council of ministers as per Article 164?

• The minimum number of ministers in the council of ministers, including the Chief Minister, cannot be less than **12**.
 
• The ceiling of 15% applies only to the legislative assembly and not to the legislative council (if present in the state).

questions.question: The Third Schedule of the Indian Constitution contains which of the following?

__
 
• The Third Schedule of the Indian Constitution contains **the Forms of Oaths or Affirmations** for various constitutional posts.
 
• These oaths or affirmations are administered to **constitutional functionaries** such as the President, Vice-President, Ministers, Members of Parliament, Members of State Legislatures, Judges of the Supreme Court, and Judges of High Courts.
 
• The purpose of these oaths is to ensure that individuals occupying constitutional posts commit to **upholding the Constitution of India** and discharging their duties faithfully.
 
• The text of the oaths emphasizes allegiance to the Constitution, sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India, along with adherence to laws.
 
• The process and wording of these oaths are legally binding and are conducted in accordance with the provisions set out in the Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Union List, State List, and Concurrent List:**

 
 
• The Union List and State List are mentioned in the **Seventh Schedule** of the Indian Constitution, not the Third Schedule.
 
• The Union List includes subjects under the exclusive legislative domain of the Parliament, while the State List includes subjects for state legislatures. The Concurrent List includes subjects where both Parliament and state legislatures can legislate.
 
 
 
• **Recognized Languages:**
 
 
• The recognized languages of India are enumerated in the **Eighth Schedule** of the Constitution.
 
• The Eighth Schedule originally listed 14 languages, but now it includes **22 officially recognized languages**.
 
 
 
• **Oath Taking Process:**

• Governors administer the oath to Chief Ministers and other state ministers.

• Article 60 of the Constitution prescribes the oath or affirmation for the President of India.
 
• Article 124(6) prescribes the oath for Supreme Court judges, and Article 219 for High Court judges.

questions.question: Which Schedule of the Indian Constitution was added to prevent defection of elected members?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tenth Schedule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Tenth Schedule of the Indian Constitution, popularly known as the **Anti-Defection Law**, was added by the **52nd Amendment Act of 1985**.
 
• It was introduced to prevent **political defections** by elected members of the legislature.
 
• The law specifies the conditions under which a member of a legislature can be disqualified on grounds of defection.
 
• Defection occurs when a legislator either voluntarily resigns from their party or votes/abstains contrary to the party's directives.
 
• The authority to decide disqualification under the Tenth Schedule lies with the **Chairman or Speaker** of the respective House.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Background of Anti-Defection Law:**

 
 
• Political defections in India were rampant during the 1960s and 70s, leading to instability in governments.
 
• The Anti-Defection Law was enacted to address this issue and ensure political stability and discipline among elected representatives.
 
 
 
• **Exceptions under the Tenth Schedule:**
 
 
• Members are not disqualified if their party merges with another and at least two-thirds of its members agree to the merger.
 
• An independent legislator can join a party within six months of being elected without being disqualified.
 
 
 
• **Recent Developments:**
 
 
• The Anti-Defection Law has faced criticism for vesting decision-making power solely in the Speaker, raising concerns about impartiality.
 
• Some experts advocate for the establishment of an independent body to decide disqualification cases.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Law:**
 
 
• It has helped reduce the frequency of defections and brought greater stability to Indian legislatures.
 
• However, it has also been criticized for restricting lawmakers' ability to express dissent freely.

questions.question: Which Schedule of the Constitution of India deals with the allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha to states and union territories?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Fourth Schedule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Fourth Schedule** of the Constitution of India deals with the allocation of seats in the **Rajya Sabha (Council of States)** to various states and union territories.
 
• It specifies the number of seats each state and union territory is entitled to, based on their **population**.
 
• The allocation is done in a way to ensure proportional representation of states and union territories in the Rajya Sabha.
 
• The Fourth Schedule is mentioned in **Articles 4(1) and 80(2)** of the Constitution of India.
 
• Representation in the Rajya Sabha is not uniform; it is designed to reflect the federal structure of India, ensuring that larger states have more representation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Rajya Sabha (Council of States):**

 
 
• It is the upper house of the Indian Parliament, representing the states and union territories of India.
 
• Members are elected by the legislative assemblies of states and union territories through a proportional representation system.
 
• The Rajya Sabha has a maximum strength of **250 members**, of which 12 are nominated by the President for their contributions to art, literature, science, and social services.
 
 
 
• **Proportional Representation:**
 
 
• This system ensures that the number of seats allocated to each state or union territory in the Rajya Sabha corresponds to its population size.
 
• It promotes equitable representation while acknowledging the diversity of India's federal structure.
 
 
 
• **Union Territories in the Rajya Sabha:**
 
 
• Not all union territories have representation in the Rajya Sabha; only those with legislative assemblies (e.g., Delhi, Puducherry) are allocated seats.
 
• The allocation of seats for union territories is also specified in the Fourth Schedule.
 
 
 
• **Article 80 of the Constitution:**
 
 
• It lays down the composition of the Rajya Sabha, including the allocation of seats to states and union territories.
 
• The President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha based on their expertise in specific fields.
 
 
 
• **Amendments to the Fourth Schedule:**
 
 
• The Fourth Schedule can be amended through a constitutional amendment to reflect changes in the population or new states/union territories.
 
• Changes are made based on the recommendations of the Delimitation Commission.

questions.question: The distribution of powers between the Union and the States in terms of the Union List, State List and Concurrent List is under which Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Seventh Schedule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Seventh Schedule** of the Indian Constitution defines the distribution of powers between the Union and the States in terms of three lists: the **Union List, State List, and Concurrent List**.
 
• The Union List includes subjects on which only the Parliament can legislate, such as defense, foreign affairs, and atomic energy.
 
• The State List includes subjects on which only the State Legislatures can legislate, such as police, public health, and agriculture.
 
• The Concurrent List includes subjects on which both the Parliament and the State Legislatures can legislate, such as education, forests, and marriage laws.
 
• This distribution of powers ensures a clear demarcation of legislative responsibilities and promotes cooperative federalism in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Union List**

 
 
• Contains **97 subjects** originally (now 100 after amendments).
 
• Examples include defense, foreign affairs, banking, and atomic energy.
 
• Parliament has exclusive authority to make laws on these subjects.
 
 
 
• **State List**
 
 
• Originally contained **66 subjects** (now 61 after amendments).
 
• Examples include police, public health, and agriculture.
 
• State Legislatures have exclusive authority to legislate on these subjects.
 
 
 
• **Concurrent List**
 
 
• Originally contained **47 subjects** (now 52 after amendments).
 
• Examples include education, forests, and marriage laws.
 
• Both Parliament and State Legislatures can legislate on these subjects; however, in case of conflict, the law made by Parliament prevails.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context**
 
 
• The concept of the division of powers was borrowed from the **Government of India Act, 1935**.
 
• This framework ensures a balance between centralization and decentralization in governance.

questions.question: The list of all official languages is given in which Schedule of the Indian Constitution?

The correct answer is __**Schedule 8**__.

__
 
• Schedule 8 of the Indian Constitution lists the **official languages** recognized by the Government of India.
 
• Initially, Schedule 8 contained **14 languages** when the Constitution was adopted in 1950.
 
• Currently, the Schedule includes a total of **22 languages**, following amendments made to the Constitution over time.
 
• The official languages listed in Schedule 8 include Hindi, Bengali, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, Urdu, and several others.
 
• Languages in Schedule 8 are entitled to development under Article 344 and Article 351 of the Indian Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Amendments:** Languages such as Sindhi, Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali, Bodo, Santhali, Maithili, and Dogri were added through Constitutional Amendments (e.g., the 21st, 71st, and 92nd Amendments).
 
• **Linguistic Diversity:** India is a multilingual nation, and the inclusion of languages in Schedule 8 is aimed at preserving its rich linguistic heritage.
 
• **Official Language Act 1963:** This Act ensures the continued use of English alongside Hindi for official purposes, addressing the linguistic diversity of the country.

questions.question: The Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution deals with ____________.

options.text: administration and control of scheduled areas and scheduled tribes

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**administration and control of scheduled areas and scheduled tribes**__.

__
 
• The Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution deals specifically with **the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes**.
 
• It provides for the establishment of a **Tribes Advisory Council (TAC)** in each state having scheduled areas, comprising members of the Scheduled Tribes in the legislative assembly.
 
• The President of India is empowered to **declare any area as a Scheduled Area** and can also alter or rescind such declarations.
 
• The Governor of the state is responsible for submitting an **annual report** to the President regarding the administration of Scheduled Areas.
 
• The Fifth Schedule emphasizes the **protection of tribal rights** over land and resources and ensures their **cultural and economic development**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Scheduled Areas**:

 
 
• These are defined under the Fifth Schedule as areas with a significant population of Scheduled Tribes.
 
• The criteria include geographical isolation, economic backwardness, and distinct social customs, traditions, and practices.
 
 
 
• **Tribes Advisory Council (TAC)**:
 
 
• A constitutional body established to advise on the welfare and advancement of Scheduled Tribes in the state.
 
• It consists of not more than 20 members, with three-fourths being representatives of the Scheduled Tribes in the Legislative Assembly.
 
 
 
• **Governor’s Role**:
 
 
• The Governor has special responsibilities for the governance of Scheduled Areas and is empowered to make regulations restricting the transfer of tribal land to non-tribals.
 
• They can also regulate the allotment of land to STs and the management of their resources.
 
 
 
• **Sixth Schedule**:
 
 
• While the Fifth Schedule focuses on Scheduled Areas and Tribes, the Sixth Schedule deals with the administration of tribal areas in the northeastern states like Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram.
 
• It provides for autonomous district councils with legislative, judicial, and administrative powers.

• **Constituent Assembly of India:**

• **Objective Resolution:**

questions.question: Nehru asserted that the Constituent Assembly derived its strength primarily from

• Nehru saw the Assembly as a representation of India's struggle for independence and its commitment to establishing a democratic and inclusive governance system.
 
• The Indian Constitution was drafted to reflect the aspirations of millions of Indians, marking a significant break from colonial administrative frameworks.

questions.question: The Preamble of the Indian Constitution was amended in 1976 to include which of the following words?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Preamble of the Indian Constitution was amended by the **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, during the Emergency period.
 
• Two words, **"Socialist"** and **"Secular"**, were added to the Preamble to emphasize the commitment to social justice and religious neutrality.
 
• The amendment was enacted under the leadership of then Prime Minister **Indira Gandhi**.
 
• The term "Socialist" was included to reflect the government's aim to reduce income inequality and ensure equitable distribution of wealth.
 
• The term "Secular" was added to affirm India's commitment to religious freedom and equality for all religions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **42nd Amendment Act, 1976:**
 
 
• Often referred to as the "Mini-Constitution" due to its extensive changes to the Constitution.
 
• It also added "Integrity" to the phrase "Unity and Integrity of the Nation" in the Preamble.
 
 
 
• **Socialist:**
 
 
• The term emphasizes reducing economic inequality and promoting social justice.
 
• It does not imply complete state ownership but rather a mixed economy with state and private participation.
 
 
 
• **Secular:**

• The President of India is the** chief executive authority of a Union Territory**.
 
• The President acts through an administrator appointed by them, who may be designated as Lieutenant Governor or Administrator. 
 
• The President of India is the constitutional head of the country.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• However, the Chief Minister does not have authority over **police, public order, and land**, which are controlled by the Lieutenant Governor.
 
• Delhi's governance structure is unique, as it combines features of a **Union Territory** and a partially autonomous state.
 
 
 
• **The Prime Minister**__
 __

• The Lieutenant Governor has the authority to oversee the implementation of laws and policies in Delhi, especially in matters related to police, public order, and land.
 
• While Delhi has a Chief Minister and a government elected by the people, the Lieutenant Governor holds substantial administrative powers and acts as a bridge between the state government and the central government.
 
• The role of the Lieutenant Governor in Delhi is governed by the Government of NCT of Delhi Act, 1991 and subsequent amendments.
 
• In case of conflict between the elected government and the Lieutenant Governor, the matter can be referred to the President of India for resolution.
 
• The Lieutenant Governor also oversees important agencies such as the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) and other administrative bodies in the Union Territory.

questions.question: Which of the following Acts provided for the establishment of a federal, provincial and joint public service commission, Reserve Bank of India and a federal court?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Government of India Act, 1935**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Government of India Act, 1935** is one of the most significant constitutional developments in Indian history.
 
• It provided for the establishment of a **federal system** in India, which included a federal, provincial, and joint public service commission.
 
• This Act also paved the way for the creation of the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** to regulate currency and credit in the country.
 
• It introduced the concept of a **Federal Court of India**, which was a precursor to the present-day Supreme Court of India.
 
• The Act divided powers between the **Centre and the Provinces**, marking a significant step toward provincial autonomy.
 
• It abolished the **diarchy system** at the provincial level and introduced it at the central level.
 
• It also extended the scope of representative government by increasing the size of the electorate.
 
• The Act was the longest legislation enacted by the British Parliament at that time, consisting of **321 sections and 10 schedules**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Government of India Act, 1919**__

 __
 
• This Act is also known as the **Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms.**
 
• It introduced the system of **diarchy** (dual governance) in provinces, wherein subjects were divided into 'reserved' and 'transferred' categories.
 
• The Act sought to increase **Indian participation** in governance but fell short of meeting nationalist aspirations.
 
• It also provided for a bicameral legislature at the center, consisting of the **Council of State** and the **Legislative Assembly.**
 
 
 
• **Government of India Act, 1929**__
 __
 
• This Act does not exist as a separate legislation. The reference might be a misunderstanding or confusion with the **Simon Commission**, which was appointed in 1927 and submitted its report in 1930.
 
• The Simon Commission's recommendations eventually led to the drafting of the **Government of India Act, 1935.**
 
 
 
• **Government of India Act, 1909**__
 
 
• This Act is commonly known as the **Morley-Minto Reforms.**
 
• It introduced the concept of **separate electorates** for Muslims, which sowed the seeds of communal politics in India.
 
• The Act aimed to increase **Indian representation** in legislative councils but was limited in scope.
 
• It also increased the number of **elected members** in provincial and central legislative councils.

questions.question: According to the Constitution, which body is responsible for creating or abolishing a legislative council in a state?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The Parliament of India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• According to Article 169 of the Indian Constitution, the legislative council in a state can be created or abolished by the **Parliament of India** upon receiving a recommendation from the state legislative assembly.
 
• The resolution recommending the creation or abolition of the legislative council must be passed in the state assembly by a **special majority** (not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting).
 
• The legislative council, also known as the Vidhan Parishad, is the **upper house** in the bicameral legislature of certain states.
 
• Currently, only a few states in India, such as Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana, have a legislative council.
 
• The Parliament's decision on the creation or abolition of a legislative council is implemented via an amendment to the **Legislative Councils Act** of the concerned state.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad):**

 
 
• It is a permanent body that cannot be dissolved, but one-third of its members retire every two years.
 
• Members are elected through various methods, including elections by legislative assembly members, graduates, teachers, and local authority representatives.
 
• The total number of members in a legislative council cannot exceed one-third of the strength of the state legislative assembly.
 
 
 
• **Article 169:**
 
 
• This article empowers the Parliament to create or abolish legislative councils in states based on state assembly resolutions.
 
• It specifies the process through which the state assembly can make a recommendation to Parliament.
 
 
 
• **Bicameral Legislature:**
 
 
• States with a bicameral legislature have both the Vidhan Sabha (Legislative Assembly) and Vidhan Parishad (Legislative Council).
 
• Bicameral legislatures exist in fewer states compared to unicameral systems, where only the Vidhan Sabha exists.
 
 
 
• **Current Status:**
 
 
• As of now, six states in India have legislative councils, while the rest have unicameral legislatures.
 
• Recent debates have surfaced regarding the abolition or creation of legislative councils in various states.

__
 
• The **President of India** is elected indirectly by an **electoral college** as per Article 55 of the **Indian Constitution**.
 
• The electoral college consists of elected representatives from both **Houses of Parliament** (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) and the elected members of the **Legislative Assemblies of States** (including Union Territories with legislatures).
 
• The process is governed under the provisions of the **Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952**.
 
• The election is conducted through a system of **proportional representation** using a **single transferable vote**.
 
• The value of votes is calculated based on the population of states as per the **1971 Census** and the number of elected representatives.
 
• The election ensures a balance between representation from the **Union Parliament** and the **State Legislatures**.
 
• The voting takes place through a **secret ballot** to uphold the integrity of the election process.
 
• The President serves as the **head of the state** and the **supreme commander of the Indian Armed Forces**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 __

• **State Governors**__
 __

questions.question: Who's assent is required for the Constitutional Amendment Bill to become an Act?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**The President of India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **Constitutional Amendment Bill** in India is introduced to make changes to the provisions of the **Indian Constitution**.
 
• Once the amendment bill is passed by both the **Houses of Parliament** (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) with the required majority, it is sent to the **President of India** for their assent.
 
• The role of the President is crucial, as the bill becomes an **Act** only after the President's signature.
 
• The Constitution of India does not provide the President with the option to return the bill or withhold their assent; they are bound to give their approval once the bill is duly passed.
 
• The process is governed by **Article 368** of the Indian Constitution, which details the procedure for amending the Constitution.
 
• Unlike ordinary bills, Constitutional Amendment Bills do not require the assent of the **Governor** or involvement of the **State Legislatures** unless the amendment affects their powers.
 
• This process ensures that any change to the Constitution undergoes rigorous scrutiny and is approved by a consensus of the legislature and the President.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Prime Minister of India**__

 __
 
• The **Prime Minister** is the head of the government and plays a key role in the legislative process, but their assent is not required for Constitutional Amendment Bills to become an Act.
 
• They may propose or support amendments, but the final approval lies with the **President of India**.
 
 
 
• **Chief Justice of India**__
 __
 
• The **Chief Justice of India** heads the judiciary and ensures the Constitution is upheld, but they do not have a direct role in the legislative process of passing or amending bills.
 
• Judicial review can be applied to determine the validity of an amendment, but their assent is not part of the procedure.
 
 
 
• **The Speaker of Lok Sabha**__
 
 
• The **Speaker of Lok Sabha** oversees proceedings within the Lok Sabha, including discussions and voting on bills.
 
• While their role is important in facilitating the passage of the bill in the Lok Sabha, they do not provide assent for Constitutional Amendment Bills to become an Act.

questions.question: Who among the following appoints the Administrator of a Union Territory without a Legislative Assembly?

• The **President of India** appoints the Administrator of a Union Territory (UT) without a Legislative Assembly under Article 239 of the Indian Constitution.

• In Union Territories without Legislative Assemblies (e.g., Lakshadweep, Andaman & Nicobar Islands), the Administrator primarily governs the territory on behalf of the Central Government.
 
• The appointment of the Administrator is done by the President, ensuring that the administration aligns with the policies and interests of the Central Government.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• Some UTs like Delhi and Puducherry have Legislative Assemblies, while others do not.
 
 
 
• **Article 239 of the Constitution:**
 
 
• This article empowers the President to appoint an Administrator for Union Territories.
 
• The Administrator is responsible for implementing laws and policies in the UT.
 
 
 
• **Role of the Administrator:**
 
 
• The Administrator functions under the direct control of the Central Government.
 
• They are responsible for law and order, governance, and overall administration of the UT.

questions.question: Which Prime Minister’s 'Inner Cabinet' became particularly powerful during their era?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Indira Gandhi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• During Indira Gandhi's tenure as Prime Minister, her 'Inner Cabinet' or 'Kitchen Cabinet' became extremely powerful and influential in decision-making.
 
• The Inner Cabinet consisted of a small group of trusted advisors and ministers who played a significant role in shaping policies and bypassing the regular Cabinet structure.
 
• Prominent members of this informal group included individuals like P.N. Haksar, who served as her principal secretary and was instrumental in policy formulation.
 
• This structure allowed Indira Gandhi to centralize power, reducing the influence of senior Congress leaders and making her governance more authoritarian in nature.
 
• The dominance of the Inner Cabinet was especially evident during critical events like the nationalization of banks in 1969 and the declaration of Emergency in 1975.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kitchen Cabinet:**

 
 
• An informal group of advisors or ministers who work closely with the head of the government, often bypassing the formal Cabinet system.
 
• Such groups are not officially recognized but wield significant influence over policymaking and decision-making processes.
 
 
 
• **Centralization of Power:**
 
 
• Indira Gandhi's leadership style was marked by a strong centralization of authority, reducing the autonomy of regional Congress leaders and state governments.
 
• This centralization was often criticized for undermining democratic institutions and fostering authoritarian practices.
 
 
 
• **Bank Nationalization of 1969:**
 
 
• One of the landmark decisions during Indira Gandhi's tenure, where 14 major private banks were nationalized to bring banking services to the masses.
 
• The decision was heavily influenced by her Inner Cabinet and marked a shift towards socialist economic policies.
 
 
 
• **Emergency Period (1975-1977):**
 
 
• During this period, democratic processes were suspended, and civil liberties were curtailed under Indira Gandhi's leadership.
 
• The decision to impose Emergency was driven by her close advisors, showcasing the power of the Inner Cabinet.
 
 
 
• **P.N. Haksar's Role:**
 
 
• As Indira Gandhi's principal secretary, P.N. Haksar played a pivotal role in shaping key policies, including the abolition of privy purses and the nationalization of banks.
 
• He was considered a key member of her Inner Cabinet and a trusted confidant.
